t: This manual provides facility personnel with administrative and operational guidance governing the operation of the Marine Corps Air Station Camp Pendleton Air Traffic Control Facility.

This manual applies to all air traffic control personnel assigned to MCAS Camp Pendleton. This manual is not intended to supersede any portion of FAAO JO 7110.65 (series), or applicable Navy directives that govern air traffic control procedures. All members of the ATC facility will adhere to the provisions contained within this manual and shall exercise their best judgment should they encounter situations not specifically covered.
MCAS Camp Pendleton Air Traffic Control Facility Manual, March 2024.

a. The ATCFO is responsible for keeping this manual updated with current procedures, changes, and directives. b. Recommended changes shall be submitted through the TSO to the ATCFO for final approval. c. Procedures Evaluation Board (PEB) 1. PEB’s shall be conducted as outlined in the NAVAIR 00-80T-114. 2. The TSO or Training Chief shall be the chairperson of the PEB. d. This manual shall be reviewed and updated annually. In reviewing this manual, all applicable letters of agreement shall be reviewed for accuracy and conformance with current policy. In conjunction with the annual review, Branch Chiefs will incorporate any necessary updates or changes to the simulator training program. Additions or deletions to this manual will be issued as facility directives, facility memorandums and facility manual change notices.

a. Hard copies of current facility directives are maintained in the facility manual binder within each branch. Digital files are also maintained in the ATC Digital Library located on Microsoft Teams, channel name ‘ATC Publications’. These directives are published to outline details of any new procedures not yet incorporated into the Facility Manual. b. The information board is in the brief room. This board contains information of general interest to all personnel such as duty assignments, administrative notes, etc.
The uniform of the day is prescribed by the MCAS Commanding Officer.

Field day shall be accomplished weekly unless otherwise directed. Crew Chiefs will ensure that proper field day is completed prior to close of business (Tower, Radar, brief room, admin offices, head across from radar room, front entry way of building 2399).

The control tower and radar facilities are designated restricted areas. No photographs are allowed without permission of the MCAS Commanding Officer. Visitors may be allowed with the consent of the ATCFO or designated representative. Visitors will sign the visitor log located in the ATC brief room and always remain with their sponsors to preclude any interference with ATC operations.

The telephones in both the radar room and tower are to be used for official business only. Under no circumstances will these phone numbers be given out to anyone who does not work in ATC. Telephonic threat forms are in the TS / RS binders. Any request for information concerning any incident will be directed to the Public Affairs Office (PAO) at 725-5011. At no time will operational information be released without approval of the FWO, nor should personal information be given out. This includes work schedules, personal phone numbers, etc.

a. Leave requests will be submitted to the SNCOIC via the Crew Chief/designated representative through Marine Online at least five working days in advance of the leave date and shall be accompanied by a HARP form. All leave requests shall be discussed with the Crew Chief for potential staffing or training impacts. b. Civilian leave requests will be submitted to the ATCFO or TSO via DAI five working days in advance. For emergency or sick leave, notify the ATCFO or TSO as soon as able. c. Students shall take extra consideration when submitting leave while training at percentages of 75% and higher. These leave requests will be approved by the ATCFO on a case-by-case basis. If the leave period will significantly negatively impact the students training or qualification timeline, the student should expect to defer the leave period to a later date. This shall not apply to emergency leave, Christmas, or religious holidays. d. Liberty is in accordance with the watch schedule or as authorized by the crew officer. e. During normal working hours, emergency leave will be handled by the Crew Chief or designated representative.

The facility operates on a rotating crew schedule every two weeks. The watch schedule, crew assignments, and civilian work schedules will be maintained on the facility Teams page and distributed electronically. All efforts will be made by Marines to schedule annual and fiscal year training in a manner that does not impede on facility training.

a. Food and drink are authorized in the tower and radar room provided the following is adhered to: 1. Drinks shall be in spill proof containers. 2. Food is authorized in the tower and radar room only if personnel shortages dictate. b. Smoking is only authorized in designated areas at least 50 feet from building entrances and air intake ducts and will not be in areas commonly used by nonsmokers. The term “smoking” includes the use of e-cigarettes and all new and emergent tobacco products such as cigarettes, cigars, little cigars, pipe tobacco, roll-your-own tobacco, and electronic nicotine delivery systems. c. Use of television is not permitted in either control room.

a. Controller of the Quarter 1. Recognition of skilled professionals is essential. The primary avenue for recognizing outstanding performance within the ATC facility is the Controller of the Quarter board. 2. A Controller of the quarter board will convene at the beginning of April, July and October, and mid-November. The ATC SNCOIC is responsible for assembling the board and forwarding a recommendation to the ATCFO for final selection. Examples of achievements that warrant nomination are contained in the reference. The following procedures apply to the nomination and selection process: (a) All air traffic control personnel assigned to this command during the quarter are eligible. Facility Introduction - General JULY 2026 NFG FACMAN (b) Period of consideration is the first through the last working day of the quarter. Nominations shall be submitted five working days prior to the convening date of the board. (c) Any air traffic controller may submit a nomination; however, it shall be submitted via the Crew Chief/Crew Officer. (d) Nominations shall be made in writing and forwarded via the chain of command. All nominations shall contain a detailed summary of the nominee’s actions. (e) Selection will be based on the action summary and individual training record. b. Selectees from each quarter will compete for the distinction of Controller of the Year, MCAS Camp Pendleton. The Controller of the Quarter Board, fourth quarter will make the Controller of the Year recommendation to the ATCFO to be considered for the Admiral Robert B. Pirie Naval Air Traffic Controller of the Year Award. REFERENCENAVAIR 00-80T-114 Para 4.4.4, Annual Awards

MCAS Camp Pendleton provides operating forces and tenant organizations with continuous and effective aviation service and support; ensuring their ability to respond to present and emerging national defense requirements. We utilize dedicated professionalism, a can-do work ethic and innovative technology to attain the best possible support services, better enabling our customers to accomplish their mission.

The mission of the Air Traffic Control Facility is to provide for the safe, orderly, and expeditious movement of air traffic, including aircraft movement on the ground, to and from the airport, and within assigned airspace, and to interface with the National Airspace System.

a. Our mission should reflect in all that we do. b. Our controllers are our most important assets. We provide a professional working environment that ensures the dignity of our controllers, encourages them to develop their skills, promotes job pride and satisfaction, and rewards initiative and improvement. c. Listen to your seniors and subordinates. Encourage participation in decision-making. Promote and recognize teamwork in our efforts. d. Don’t be afraid of change. Look for better ways to get the job done. If current policies and processes don’t make sense, ask questions, and make suggestions for improvement. e. Focus on quality; don’t settle for good enough. Provide the best service you can, and train to produce the best controllers possible to support the Air Station and the MOS. If something is broken, start fixing it. f. Provide training opportunities; support the concept of “train for the future.” g. Personally lead, and reward excellence.

Provide the best possible service and information to the aircrews we serve. No controller in this facility, regardless of rank, shall be anything but respectful, courteous, and professional. If pilots / aircrews are abusive or have unrealistic requests, attempt to professionally approve or deny the request, then notify the chain of command.

The Marine Corps Air Station provides arrival and departure control, GCA radar service, and tower control service to aircraft operating within Class D and E airspace. In addition, flight planning and approval services are conducted by Marine Corps personnel. Southern California TRACON (SCT), by letter of agreement, has delegated the airspace known as Lima and Golf (see Appendix C) to MCAS Camp Pendleton. This airspace is controlled by GCA and provides IFR approach control and departure control services to aircraft operating to / from the air station and Fallbrook Airpark. MCAS Camp Pendleton is located six miles north of the city of Oceanside, California, and situated on the 028 degree radial at 5 nautical miles from the Oceanside VORTAC. The latitude and longitude for the Airport Reference Point (ARP) is 33°18’04.53” north, 117°21’18.61” west. The field elevation is 78 feet above sea level. The airfield is located within mountainous terrain.

The airport is situated in a valley, oriented northeast to southwest approximately 7 miles long and 2 ½ to 3 miles wide with surrounding foothills at an elevation of 100 to 500 feet. The weather in the Camp Pendleton area is mainly controlled by the Pacific Ocean to the west and the Santa Margarita mountains to the east. The ocean tends to moderate temperatures in the lower layers of the atmosphere due to the sea breeze, while the mountains to the east act as a barrier between the desert and coastal area thus giving a drying effect to the easterly flow. The relationship between these air masses creates a semi-permanent low-level inversion over the local area that creates conditions conducive to the formation of low stratus and fog. However, during the winter these conditions are occasionally interrupted by frontal passage and highly modified air masses.

MCB has delegated the airspace identified as Class D and E to MCAS as described in the reference. The MCAS Camp Pendleton Class D airspace is the circular airspace extending from the surface up to and including 2600 feet MSL. This airspace extends from the ARP to the following points: the 010 bearing at 4NM clockwise to the 227 bearing at 4NM direct to the 240 bearing at 2.6NM clockwise to the 355 bearing at 2.6NM direct to the 010 bearing at 4NM (See also Appendix C). REFERENCEFAAO JO 7400.11, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points

The MCAS Camp Pendleton Class E airspace extends from the surface up to and including 2600 feet MSL. This airspace is a continuation of Class D extending from the 010 bearing at 4 NM direct to the 018 bearing at 6.9 NM direct to the 041 bearing at 6.9 NM direct to the 050 bearing at 4 NM (See also Appendix C).

a. BASIC VFR MINIMA. VFR minima are established as a ceiling not less than 1000 feet AGL and/or visibility not less than 3 statute miles. b. LESS THAN VFR MINIMA. When the reported ceiling and/or visibility are less than basic VFR minima, all flight operations shall be conducted in accordance with SVFR/IFR procedures. SVFR clearance requires a minimum of 1 statute mile visibility and clear of clouds while in the Class D surface area. Minima for IFR departures and landings are contained in appropriate radar and instrument approach procedure publications. c. SVFR MINIMA. The minima depend on the route requested or the operation being conducted. See Paragraph 5-1-7. REFERENCE-US Code of Federal Regulations, Part 91 Administration - General JULY 2026 NFG FACMAN d. AIRFIELD MINIMA. The minima for arrivals are the published approach ceiling and visibility for the approach being conducted. Minimums for departure are specified by NAVAIR 00-80T-114. If weather conditions are below the minima for the approach requested, the controller will ensure that the pilot has the current official reported weather. If the pilot still wants the approach, a clearance will be issued by the controlling authority. An entry will be made in the Facility Log and an Incident report generated. This report will be forwarded to Airfield Operations via the ATCFO for determination. See Chapter 2, Section 3 of this manual for the handling of operational hazards. REFERENCE-CNAF M-3710.7 Para 5.3, Instrument Flight Rules and Positive Control Procedures

a. TRANSIENT SERVICES. 1. VISITING AIRCRAFT LINE (VAL). This section is located in the Flight Clearance office. The services include aircraft parking utilizing Beast 11. Aircraft hangar space for transient aircraft is not available. Tie down parking spaces are extremely limited. Prior Permission is Required (PPR) from Airfield Operations for transient aircraft. Exceptions to the PPR requirement are emergency aircraft and transient aircraft being hosted by a tenant squadron. Transient civil aircraft and military charter aircraft shall possess a MCAS Camp Pendleton facility license or be a member of a recognized military flying club. 2. MAINTENANCE. The airfield does not have an aircraft maintenance section. Transient aircraft may be provided with limited services during normal working hours by tenant units. b. FLIGHT PLANNING. Complete flight planning and clearance service facilities are available during normal airfield hours. Flight Clearance has been assigned a UHF frequency of 279.3. c. AIRCRAFT RESCUE AND FIRE FIGHTING (ARFF). ARFF at Camp Pendleton is Category II. Categories are determined by size and type of aircraft on the line. Camp Pendleton can handle all aircraft. The basic purpose of the ARFF section is to provide crash rescue service to all aircraft, regardless of type, which may land at Camp Pendleton. ARFF is manned on a 24-hour basis and posts immediate response vehicles during field hours. ARFF has the secondary function of assisting the base fire department as necessary. d. WEATHER. The weather section is part of the National Weather Service (NWS) system. They prepare and disseminate local area weather reports to the NWS and to pilots during pilot weather briefings. Weather services are provided locally during airfield hours and at other times are available through MCAS Miramar on METRO frequency 342.4. e. ATC MAINTENANCE DIVISION (ATCMD). ATCMD is responsible for the maintenance of NAVAIDS, radar, and communications equipment for the facility. Technicians are available during field hours.

Hydraulic emergency: 1. UH-1/AH-1. Flight control hydraulic system failures will result in degradation of aircraft control. In addition, the pooling of hydraulic fluid in the aircraft poses a chance of fire. A single system failure will result in some degradation of aircraft control, but the aircraft will remain controllable in most normal flight regimes and conditions. Aircrew will normally request a straight-in approach to the runway and landing on the runway. A dual or two system flight control hydraulic systems failure is an acute problem for the aircrew because the condition significantly reduces the aircrew’s capacity to control the aircraft. Aircrew will normally request a long straight-in approach and perform a sliding landing to the runway. Aircrew will normally keep the aircraft descent rate low, between 200 – 300 feet per minute and between 40 and 60 knots. Aircraft will require tow. 2. Fixed wing. Hydraulic system failures affect several systems for the aircrew; there will be some degradation in aircraft handling (like losing power steering in a car). More time is required for aircraft to lower landing gear and go through landing checklist. Pooling of hydraulic fluid in the aircraft poses a chance of fire. Aircrew will normally request a visual check of the aircraft’s landing gear by the controller. Aircraft will require a tow. b. Chip warning light. This indicates the presence of foreign metal matter in either the engine, transmission, or other gear boxes. The aircrew may request to land as soon as possible due to possible aircraft engine, transmission, or gear box failure. It should be noted that in some cases this type of indication is not to be considered an actual emergency. Confirm with the pilot if they desire to declare an emergency. c. The goal of the ATC training program is to produce the highest-quality, most proficient controllers while reducing qualification times and trainee downtime. The program is built on a crawl / walk / run design and should be regularly measured, analyzed, and improved. Critical elements of the program include academic instruction, simulation training, familiarization training, and on-the-job training (OJT). The program contains the minimum requirements to produce either a Local Controller (7252) or Arrival / Departure Controller (7253). These qualifications also prepare the Marine for service in the Fleet Marine Force. The Training and Readiness (T&R) Manual requires all Marines to earn two qualifications (GC & FD or FC & RD) within the first 12 months of arriving at their first ATC Facility; Marines are also required to earn NMOS 7252 or 7253 within 3 years of arriving at their first facility. Only higher headquarters can approve waivers to these standards. Position training is accomplished in three phases. The training team shall record the beginning and end of each training phase on the trainee’s eval. a. ACADEMIC AND SIMULATION PHASE. Trainees will complete all position tests and receive simulations to reinforce the material. Required simulations must be completed for each test prior to taking the next test. Trainees shall not proceed to the next phase without completing this training phase. During this training phase, students shall take at least one test and complete all associated simulations each week. Three hours of simulation (or 50 simulated approaches) are required during each week of this phase. b. ON-THE-JOB FAMILIARIZATION (OJF) PHASE. This phase of training should be no longer than one week in duration. Trainees shall receive at least ten hours of familiarization training. RFC trainees should get OJF on as many approaches as possible during the week. Training received during this phase will not count against a student’s OJT timeline. A trainee may receive direct experience in the work environment if: 1. The Branch Supervisor approves. 2. The controller responsible for the position is current and designated as an OJTI on that position. 3. The position is not combined. 4. Controllers shall not receive direct work experience on any Tower position if the field is IFR. 5. Controllers shall not receive direct work experience on any Radar position if the weather is less than 5000' ceiling or less than 5 miles visibility. 6. The controller shall not receive direct work experience without a current DD Form 2992 on file.

a. The training evaluation is a record of training used toward certification while signed on an ATC position or while training on simulators or in a classroom. A training evaluation is required for each trainee for each operating position. b. Separate training evaluation forms will be completed for each position on which the trainee trained during the week (i.e., training conducted on RD and AR during the same week). Each phase of training (testing / sim, OJF, OJT) will be documented in the appropriate section of the evaluation. c. After completion of training for the week, the training team shall document all training information on the evaluation; this shall be completed no later than Friday. The Branch Chiefs and TSO shall review and comment on the evaluation by the first workday of the following week. d. At a minimum, the following information is required on training evaluations: 1 All needs improvement and/or unsatisfactory marks shall be accompanied with a brief explanation. 2. All OJTI comments shall be strictly professional and shall emphasize constructive criticism. 3. Both the OJTI and trainee shall type their operating initials immediately following their comments. 4. Trainee comments are encouraged and may be made after being debriefed on the training session. 5. The evaluation session shall be documented as soon as possible after the training session. 6. Weekly comments shall reflect only constructive remarks and should provide a reasonable narrative of the work completed by the trainee. Comments shall not include subjective remarks like, “should be recommended soon,” “waiting to see more traffic,” or similar remarks. 7. Evaluations for tower or radar supervisor trainees should be maintained. In addition, training times will be logged on the branch supervisor’s position log. 8. By the end of the training week, the PI, TTL, trainee and Crew Chief will review and initial all appropriate evaluations. 9. “NTOP” or “other military duties” notes shall be accompanied with a justification. e. Additional guidance for completing the training evaluation is contained in NAVAIR 00-80T-114. REFERENCEInterfacility Coordination Procedures Letter of Agreement between SoCal TRACON and MCAS Camp Pendleton a. Special VFR aircraft will not be assigned fixed altitudes. The ATC tower has the authority to conduct SVFR operations at MCAS Camp Pendleton at or below 1500 feet MSL. b. SVFR operations are limited to one aircraft operating within the Class D surface area unless one of the following conditions exists: 1. Tower has all aircraft operating in Class D in sight and provides visual separation. 2. Succeeding aircraft have preceding aircraft in sight and is instructed by ATC to maintain visual separation from that aircraft. 3. With reference to IFR aircraft, coordination may be required with the RATCF prior to resuming SVFR operations to confirm position of the IFR aircraft. For example, an IFR departure leaves 1000 feet and SVFR operations are restricted at or below 500 feet. c. Special VFR operations are authorized for helicopters and V-22s in conversion mode. d. SVFR/IFR operations. IFR aircraft have priority over SVFR aircraft. When IFR aircraft are cleared for an approach into Camp Pendleton airfield while SVFR operations are being conducted, SVFR operations shall be secured, (i.e., pattern aircraft have landed and / or aircraft have reported clear of Class D) prior to the IFR aircraft reaching a 5 mile final. Exception to this rule requires the application of visual separation in accordance with FAAO JO 7110.65. e. Overflights. SVFR overflights are authorized at an altitude restriction of at or below 1500 feet MSL. CFR Part 91 requires 1 statute mile flight visibility. NAVAIR 00-80T-114 requires a 500-foot ceiling for military aircraft. REFERENCECNAF-M 3710.7 Para 5.2.4, Weather Minimums f. Special VFR Routes. Table 5-2 lists local SVFR routes. See also Appendix C. g. A Special VFR clearance may be relayed through Longrifle for those aircraft requesting clearance that are not able to establish contact with the control tower. Range Control is not authorized to issue these clearances independently and will instruct all aircraft experiencing communications difficulties to hold outside Class D airspace until a clearance can be obtained. All clearances relayed through Longrifle will be prefaced by the statement “ATC Clears…” REFERENCEJO 7110.65, Para 4-2-2, Clearance Prefix

a. When the crash phone is activated, ARFF will get into position as soon as possible. The emergency standby positions are southeast of the runway at the hold short lines of Alpha, Bravo, Delta, Echo 1 and Foxtrot 1. In addition, ground shall stop all airfield traffic. Phraseology“Attention all aircraft and vehicles, this is Camp Pendleton ground. Emergency in progress. Hold your position until further advised. Emergency in progress.” b. The ground controller will only speak to the section leader, via the TWR/GND net, to reduce frequency congestion. Relay all updated information to the command vehicle as soon as possible. See Appendix C. c. Once crash vehicles have responded, ground may allow movement on the airfield only after obtaining approval from the ARFF section leader. d. Once the emergency aircraft has landed, local may authorize rescue vehicle access onto the runway. They are required by OPNAVINST to escort the aircraft to its line. Neither pilot nor controller may override this order. If the pilot states that no further assistance is required, it shall be relayed to ARFF. The emergency aircraft shall hold its position after landing until released by the ARFF section leader. Inform the tower supervisor when the section leader advises the emergency has been secured. An entry will be made in the facility log to this effect. e. Off-station emergency procedures are as follows: 1. ARFF dispatcher will notify the tower supervisor upon change to airfield response status. (a) The tower supervisor will in turn restrict all flight operations, other than aircraft involved in support of an emergency. Tower will also ensure that Flight Clearance has been informed. (b) Flight Clearance is responsible for informing the Operations Officer, Operations Officer, or Operations SNCOIC (in the order shown) of any change in the status of the airfield. (c) This status will remain until either the Operations Officer or Airfield Operations Officer reopens or closes the airfield. 2. The ARFF section leader will contact the tower supervisor when support for operations can be met.

All VFR helicopter departures from MCAS Camp Pendleton will be in accordance with the AOM. These routes have been established by the operations department and MAG-39 as the primary routes departing Class D airspace. Approval may be made on a case-by-case basis for aircraft requesting departure routes other than those published. a. Unless operationally advantageous, all departures will be from the runway. (Helicopters cleared for takeoff from the North Grass may be instructed to proceed to the runway prior to commencing the departure). b. Consider aircraft ready for takeoff when they call for departure. Pilots are required to advise tower of any delay they may need on the runway. Aircraft may require two to five minutes on the runway for run-ups. c. VFR departures shall report departing the Class D surface area after takeoff unless otherwise specified. Aircraft desiring to stay within Class D will be monitored by the control tower. Aircraft departing via Morro Hill should be instructed to squawk VFR due to potential conflicts with other VFR & IFR traffic. d. All aircraft departing Class D intending to enter R-2503 shall contact Longrifle for clearance through the restricted area (310.3 or 123.2). e. All aircraft departing MCAS Camp Pendleton shall avoid overflying the Ranch House and the old Naval Hospital. A 1,500-foot restriction exists over Mainside, as well as a 500-foot restriction over the base stables and Naval Weapons Station. f. When runway 3 is in use and the aircraft requests multiple VFR practice approaches, unless otherwise coordinated, the aircraft will complete the circling approach, enter a right downwind, and depart via the Oceanside VORTAC or depart via Morro Hill and contact RATCF when instructed by tower. g. VFR aircraft within class D airspace requesting local GCA pattern will be coordinated from the tower to RATCF for a frequency and beacon code. Beacon codes will range from 4534 to 4543.

All IFR departures that enter SCT airspace shall be in accordance with the standard instrument departure procedures published for MCAS Camp Pendleton unless otherwise directed. a. Flight Data will request a release from Arrival Control for all IFR departures, no sooner than 5 minutes after obtaining an IFR clearance via FDIO or 5 minutes via phone from SCT. b. A release is valid for three minutes. If the aircraft has not started takeoff roll by that time, the takeoff clearance will be canceled and coordination for another release will be required. c. IFR release authority shall be obtained from Arrival Control. Arrival may authorize an IFR departure, on an individual aircraft basis, if visual separation can be applied by the tower in accordance with FAAO JO 7110.65. If the tower controller cannot provide visual separation, they will inform the arrival controller. Arrival will then become responsible for providing a release time for the departure. Arrival is not obligated to solicit releases requiring the application of visual separation. d. Departure frequencies will be assigned as follows: 1. Aircraft departing runway 21 on an IFR flight plan will be directed to contact SCT. Tower - Local Control JULY 2026 NFG FACMAN 2. Aircraft departing runway 3 on an IFR flight plan will be switched to RATCF on departure frequency 236.3 or 128.45. 3. Aircraft departing on a Corri departure shall be instructed to contact RATCF on assigned frequency. This situation is considered an emergency. Aircraft inbound with hung ordnance shall advise the tower, make a straight in approach and after landing taxi to de-arming. Aircraft with forward firing hung ordnance shall have their aircraft face 350° in the arming area. a. Pilots will: 1. Advise Camp Pendleton Tower on initial contact, stating the type of hung ordnance the aircraft has and request a straight in approach to a full stop landing. 2. After landing, hold in de-arming until the aircraft is de-armed and released by ARFF. 3. Aircraft with hung ordnance and having lost radio contact should be escorted to a final landing by a wingman. In the event that a situation arises in which an unaccompanied aircraft with hung ordnance shall recover after experiencing radio failure, the pilot will, to the maximum extent possible, avoid flying overpopulated areas while complying with lost communication procedures contained in the AOM. b. Controllers will: 1. Activate the Crash Phone and pass the standard emergency information as well as type ordnance, if known. 2. If Time Share is being conducted, advise GCA of the type aircraft, position, type ordnance and estimated arrival time. See Paragraph 6-1-13.

The Tower Supervisor (TS) is directly responsible to the FWO for all matters pertaining to air traffic control service. Primary duties are listed in NAVAIR 00-80T-114. The TS is also responsible for opening and closing procedures contained in Appendix A. Additional duties and responsibilities are contained in Chapter 2. NOTETS may be combined with FWO.

The possibility of an operational error during the first few minutes after assuming the watch is significant. The TS shall ensure watch checklists and position relief checklists are used during relief briefings. The watch checklist and position checklists are contained in Appendix A and are located at each operating position.

Ensuring sufficient personnel are on hand to staff the facility is a joint responsibility of the TS and FWO. Tower manning is considered one qualified controller for each operating position (TS, LC, FD, and GC). During limited operational periods such as weekends or holidays only, reduced manning is authorized in accordance with Paragraph 5-6-4.

FWOs may authorize the tower supervisor to combine operating positions during limited operational periods. Before combining operating positions, tower supervisors shall evaluate training schedules, projected traffic, weather conditions and controller abilities. In no case will safety of flight be compromised. The following positions may be combined: a. TS and LC b. FD / CD and GC NOTECircumstances may dictate that only one of the above positions is combined. Special consideration shall be given before combining the supervisor position; only under very limited operations should the supervisor position be combined.

The TS shall train trainees at all positions to the maximum extent practical. The TS is responsible to ensure ATC training is accomplished and is annotated on performance evaluation sheets. The TS's training responsibilities are as follows: a. Ensure that training (particularly pertinent control information) is standardized. If not, advise the tower chief or TSO and make recommendations. b. Ensure both OJT and classroom instruction are provided as trainees go through the ATC training syllabi. c. Ensure instructors provide debriefs after trainees receive time on position. Tower- Supervisor JULY 2026 NFG FACMAN

The TS is responsible for coordinating equipment outages with appropriate maintenance personnel and shall assure that an equipment checkout is performed at the beginning of each shift. They shall keep the FWO advised of operational capabilities and report malfunctions and limitations as appropriate. Complete equipment descriptions and maintenance responsibilities are covered in Chapter 8 of this manual.

This traffic signal may be overridden by the remote-control box located at the Local Control console. The control box shall be set to the ‘auto’ position during times the field is open and set to green at all other times. NOTES1. Reset procedure: from ‘red’, switch selection button to ‘green’ then back to ‘auto.’ 2. Maintenance of this light shall be conducted by Public Works (725-9803). 3. A mute button is available for times when there are multiple GCAs.

Supervisory personnel are responsible for enforcing facility directives and policies. The supervisor’s responsibility in dealing with outdated or operationally ineffective directives is to bring it to the attention of the chain of command. The Procedures Evaluation Board (PEB) is the primary method for addressing improvements to the ATC system. See Paragraph 1-1-4. Whenever safety is at stake, take appropriate action and advise the FWO and / or TSO to reevaluate the procedure.

The TS will be required to coordinate with outside agencies from time to time. The supervisors shall always present themselves as professionals during all communications. Any problems that cannot be resolved between controllers shall be brought to the attention of the FWO. Additional coordination may be required in the following areas: a. With pilots and other controllers immediately following an incident. The TS will cooperate fully when support is required for SAR or when aircraft in distress require assistance. b. Information gathering is a part of fact finding. Any internal request for information regarding an incident shall be directed to the ATCFO. No information shall be released to personnel outside the chain of command without prior coordination. Any outside request for information shall be directed to the ATCFO or SNCOIC.

The following fixes are used for reference points when coordinating with San Diego TRACON and intra-facility coordination for handoffs, point-outs, and initial approach/holding fixes. See Low Altitude FLIPs for other fixes. a. Oceanside VORTAC (OCN). NFG R-210 @ 2.3 DME. The Oceanside VORTAC is most often utilized by San Diego TRACON for holding aircraft inbound to Oceanside and Palomar Airports. Aircraft inbound from San Diego TRACON, using this point, are usually vectored Northeast at 4000 feet. Caution should be used around this area due to airway V23 crossing the OCN VORTAC NWSE. The VORTAC is not located within Lima airspace. b. BONDO. NFG R-092 @ 18.7 DME. BONDO is often utilized by San Diego TRACON for coordinating handoffs on fixed-wing aircraft from the east. BONDO is not located within Lima Airspace. c. CASPO. NFG R-031 @19 DME. ONTOS is the IAF/IF for the TACAN Z Runway 21 Approach. Aircraft handed off for the TACAN Z are normally vectored to intercept the NFG 19 DME arc prior to CASPO or for a straight-in approach. Minimum crossing altitude at CASPO is 4900 feet MSL. d. FISAM. NFG R-031 @ 10 DME. FISAM is the Final Approach Fix (FAF) for the TACAN Z Rwy 21 Approach. e. TEMEC. OCN R-026 @ 20 DME. TEMEC is the IAF for the VOR/DME or TACAN Y Runway 21 Approach. This fix is situated approximately one-tenth of a mile outside the northeastern edge of Lima airspace. Aircraft inbound for the VOR/DME or TACAN Y Runway 21 Approach will normally be vectored to intercept the OCN 20 DME arc. f. CUPIS. OCN R-026 @ 16 DME. CUPIS is the Missed Approach holding fix for the TACAN Rwy 3 Approach. CUPIS is also the coordinated non-radar holding fix with SCT. Min / max holding altitude at CUPIS is 5200 feet MSL. It is located within Lima airspace; however, the holding pattern extends into San Diego TRACON airspace. Coordination is required with San Diego TRACON for holding. g. GOZER. NFG R-083 @ 9 DME. GOZER is the Holding and IAF for the Copter TACAN RWY 21 Approach. The airspace around GOZER should be monitored for aircraft holding or departing GOZER for the Copter TACAN Rwy 21 Approach. Minimum crossing altitude at GOZER is 4200 feet MSL. Maximum holding altitude at GOZER is 6000 feet MSL; minimum is 4200 feet MSL. Radar - General JULY 2026 NFG FACMAN h. CORRI. NFG R-047 @ 9 DME. CORRI is an initial approach fix for the Copter TACAN Rwy 21 Approach and the clearance limit for the CORRI 4 departure. It is within Lima airspace, less than one mile north of Fallbrook Airpark. The following procedures shall be used: 1. At seven miles for jets, or six miles for helicopters and propeller aircraft, the final controller will activate buttons for type aircraft, duty runway, position, and intentions. Tower will respond by acknowledging the flashing plane figure. 2. At four miles for jets, or three miles for helicopters and propeller aircraft, the final controller will activate the 3/4 button. Tower will respond by acknowledging the flashing plane figure which relays the intentions. 3. The final controller will respond by acknowledging the flashing plane figure. 4. If CONT is relayed and no clearance is received by 2 miles, issue missed approach instructions unless verbal coordination is completed with the tower. 5. Any changes of aircraft intentions prior to the issuance of a clearance will be coordinated with tower flight data via the interphone. After the clearance is issued, changes shall be coordinated with the local controller. 6. Missed approaches (whether pilot- or controller-initiated) and tower clearance not received shall be coordinated via the VISCOM using the WAVE OFF button. 7. At the completion of each approach, the final controller will reset the VISCOM console by pressing the RESET button. The tower will respond by acknowledging the flashing plane figure. 8. During runway 3 operations, the final controller will initiate “circle to rwy 3” on the VIDS to signify the circling intentions to tower. Radar - Final Control JULY 2026 NFG FACMAN

When the VISCOM is out of service or unavailable, coordination for instrument approaches shall be accomplished as follows: a. At seven miles for jets, or six miles for helicopters and propeller aircraft, the final controller will coordinate with tower flight data via the interphone and pass the following information: 1. Aircraft position 2. Aircraft callsign and type 3. Intentions PHRASEOLOGY-SIX MILES, (callsign, type aircraft, intentions) b. At four miles for jets, or three miles for helicopters and propeller aircraft, the final controller will coordinate with the local controller for a clearance and pass the following information: 1. Aircraft position 2. Type aircraft 3. Intentions PHRASEOLOGY-THREE MILES, (type aircraft, intentions) 4. The local controller will respond by issuing one of the following: (a) Clearance (b) Continue (c) Wave off c. If “continue” is relayed to the final controller and no clearance is received by 2 miles, issue a missed approach instructions. d. Missed approaches (whether pilot- or controller-initiated) and tower clearance not received shall be coordinated as soon as practical. Notify the local and arrival controllers. EXAMPLE-LOCAL, P-1, (callsign) MISSED APPROACH. EXAMPLE-ARRIVAL, P-1, (callsign) MISSED APPROACH. e. Runway 3 coordination requirements are contained in Paragraph 6-4-13.

Arrival / Departure Control

The Arrival Control position shall combine arrival and departure functions for MCAS Camp Pendleton. The Arrival Controller's duties and responsibilities include, but are not limited to: a. Controlling and coordinating the movement of all instrument controlled traffic within Camp Pendleton Arrival Control area of responsibility by determining the interval to be used between successive approaches / departures; taking into consideration all aspects of the ATC situation including weather, runway in use, adequacy of NAVAIDS, reliability of communications, types of aircraft, and any other factors which may affect the overall operation. b. Issuing clearances to aircraft operating under arrival control jurisdiction. c. Initiating and accepting radar handoffs / point outs with Approach Control. d. Providing assistance and priority services to emergency aircraft. e. Maintaining radar surveillance of the MCAS Camp Pendleton Arrival Control area of responsibility and providing additional radar services, as workload permits. f. Incorporating the assistance of other operating positions within the RATCF, as necessary, to assist in the control of air traffic. NOTEThere are no restrictions on the number of aircraft permitted in the GCA pattern. It is the responsibility of each controller to know their own limitations with respect to the number of aircraft they can handle in the pattern. Each controller has the authority to limit the number of aircraft in the pattern based on their best judgment. Supervisors should be cognizant of each controller’s abilities, limitations and projected traffic when assigning positions.

Arrival controllers shall maintain an active and inactive strip board organized from bottom to top in order of priority. a. The active board shall contain flight strips on all active aircraft, to include arrivals, departures, and overflights. Strips shall be organized in the bay in the following manner from bottom to top: 1. Departures in the order released. 2. Arrivals in sequence from first to last. 3. Overflights / point outs. b. The inactive board will contain flight strips on aircraft proposed to depart Camp Pendleton or Fallbrook, aircraft with arrival estimates to Camp Pendleton or Fallbrook and aircraft with estimates to overfly the airspace.

The arrival controller is responsible for coordination necessary for the transfer of control on IFR aircraft. The Radar Flight Data controller shall complete handoffs / point outs only at the direction of the arrival controller. Radar - Arrival/Departure Control JULY 2026 NFG FACMAN

Arrival Control is responsible for the separation of all Camp Pendleton and Fallbrook IFR departures. a. Due to the close proximity of the airport to the edge of airspace boundary with SCT, all IFR aircraft departing MCAS Camp Pendleton require prior authorization from SCT. These departures will be handled as follows: 1. Tower Flight Data will call Radar Arrival/Departure Controller and request release for Camp Pendleton departures. 2. The arrival controller is responsible for initiating the release request with SCT. The request may be made by the flight data controller when directed by the arrival controller. 3. When requesting a release from SCT, the controller shall state callsign, CID, the proposed SID and amendment number with the release request. EXAMPLECAMP PENDLETON, REQUEST RELEASE (Callsign, CID and amendment number, SID). 4. Any read back of flight plan routing by SCT shall be considered a full route or amended clearance whether or not it is stated by the controller as a full route or amended clearance. The flight plan information shall be copied verbatim by controller accepting the release and forwarded to the tower as a full route or amended clearance. 5. Once the release is obtained from SCT and all conflicts have been resolved by the arrival controller, a release along with any necessary restrictions will be forwarded to the tower. EXAMPLE(Callsign, CID, restrictions, if any) RELEASED. 6. The arrival controller is responsible for coordinating with Range Air on all departures over Oceanside VORTAC. 7. When R-2503D is active with fixed-wing aircraft and the departing aircraft will overfly the Oceanside VORTAC, coordinate all IFR releases with the R-2503D controller. b. Corri Departures. IFR Departures remaining within Camp Pendleton airspace will be handled as standard IFR departures in accordance with this paragraph. c. Fallbrook departures shall be handled in accordance with the letter of agreement. SCT will call Arrival and request release for Fallbrook departures. Arrival control is the releasing authority for departures and responsible for separation between these departures and aircraft operating within Lima airspace. d. All aircraft departing runway 21 on an IFR flight plan will be directed to contact SCT on 323.0 or 127.3 when communications with the aircraft are no longer required. e. Aircraft departing runway 3 on an IFR flight plan shall be switched to Camp Pendleton Arrival (236.3 or 128.45) for sequencing and traffic advisories. A radar hand-off will be affected with SCT

a. Upwind Leg. Outbound runway heading climbing to 3000. b. Crosswind Leg. At approximately 1 NM from the end of runway 21, turn left heading 050 climbing to 3000. The crosswind vector shall not be issued until the aircraft has passed 1200 feet for runway 21 departures. c. Downwind Leg. Heading 030, parallel to the runway and final approach course. Altitude assignment will depend on MVA requirements. d. Base Leg. Heading 300-320 (100-120 for approaches from the north) at pattern altitude. e. Dogleg. Heading 210-230 (190-210 for approaches from the north) for aircraft intercepting the final approach course less than 2 miles from the approach gate. Additional intercept information is contained in FAAO JO 7110.65. f. PAR Intermediate/Final 1. The intermediate segment for the PAR is located between 11.56NM to 5.56NM from the runway point of intercept (RPI). A step down fix is located at 8.00NM from RPI. The final approach fix for the PAR is located at 5.56NM from RPI. 2. Aircraft requesting a PAR approach and within the intermediate approach segment boundaries depicted on the video map, may be descended to 2700' and 2200' as appropriate to aid in glidepath interception. g. Surveillance Approach (STARS) Intermediate/Final. Note – MAP-5 SA—21 accurately depicts the surveillance approach. MAP-1 LIMAAIR's intermediate segment shall not be used for this approach. 1. The intermediate segment for the surveillance approach (STARS) is located between 14NM to 8NM from the runway threshold (RWT). A step down fix is located at llNM from RWT. The final approach fix for the surveillance approach (STARS) is located at 8NM from RWT. 2. Aircraft requesting a surveillance approach on the STARS/ASR will not be allowed to be vectored beneath the minimum vectoring altitude with the intermediate segment that is depicted in the LIMA airspace map. To comply with the crossings restrictions associated with the intermediate, step-down and final approach fix controllers must ensure that aircraft are at the minimum vectoring altitude on their turn to final. 3. The minimum crossing altitude for the intermediate fix located l4NM from runway threshold is 3600' . The minimum crossing altitude for the stepdown fix located l1NM from RWT is 3300' REFERENCESFAAO JO 7110.65, Para 4-8-1, Approach Clearance, and FAAO JO 7110.65, Para 5-9-1, Vectors to Final Approach Course

The Radar Supervisor (RS) is directly responsible to the FWO for all matters pertaining to air traffic control service. Primary duties are listed in NAVAIR 00-80T-114. The RS is also responsible for opening and closing procedures contained in Appendix A. Additional duties and responsibilities are contained in Chapter 2 of this manual.

The possibility of an operational error during the first few minutes after assuming the watch is significant. The RS shall ensure watch checklists and position relief checklists are used during relief briefings. The watch checklist and position checklists are contained in Appendix A and are located at each operating position.

Ensuring sufficient personnel are on hand to staff the facility is a joint responsibility of the RS and FWO. Radar manning is one qualified controller for each operating position (RS, AR, RD, and 2 final controllers). During limited operational periods such as weekends or holidays, reduced manning is authorized in accordance with Paragraph 6-5-4.

FWOs may authorize the radar supervisor to combine operating positions during limited operational periods. Radar supervisors shall evaluate training schedules, projected traffic, weather conditions and controller abilities before combining operating positions. In no case will safety of flight be compromised. The following positions may be combined: a. RS with AR b. RS with RD c. AR with RD d. FC shall not be combined with any other position. NOTECircumstances may dictate that only one of the above positions is combined. Special consideration shall be given before combining the supervisor position; only under very limited operations should the supervisor position be combined. Training is not authorized during periods in which a control position is combined with any other position. Range Air may not be combined; staffing Range Air is required by letter of agreement. The Range Air controller may be relieved only by MCB range supervisory personnel. RFC may not be combined; however, staffing may be reduced to one final controller.

The RS shall train trainees at all positions to the maximum extent practical. The RS is responsible for ensuring ATC training is accomplished and is annotated on performance evaluation sheets. The RS's training responsibilities are as follows: a. Ensure that training (particularly pertinent control information) is standardized. If not, advise the radar chief or TSO and make recommendations. b. Ensure both OJT and classroom instruction are provided as trainees go through the ATC training syllabi. c. Ensure instructors provide debriefs after trainees receive time on position. Radar - Supervisor JULY 2026 NFG FACMAN d. Weather Minimums for PAR Trainees 1. Except in certain situations, PAR trainees shall not work when weather is less than 1000 feet ceiling and/or 3-mile visibility. 2. With written approval from the Radar Chief, trainees nearing qualification or who have achieved a prior RFC rating may work under supervision when weather is not less than 500 feet ceiling and/or 1-mile visibility.

The RS is responsible for coordinating equipment outages with appropriate maintenance personnel and shall assure that an equipment checkout is performed at the beginning of each shift. They shall keep the FWO advised of operational capabilities and report malfunctions and limitations as appropriate. Complete equipment descriptions and maintenance responsibilities are covered in Chapter 8 of this manual.

Supervisory personnel are responsible for enforcing facility directives and policies. The supervisor’s responsibility in dealing with outdated or operationally ineffective directives is to bring it to the attention of the chain of command. The Procedures Evaluation Board (PEB) is the primary method for addressing improvements to ATC procedures. See Paragraph 1-1-4. Whenever safety is at stake, take appropriate action deemed necessary and advise the FWO and/or TSO to reevaluate the procedure.

The RS will be required to coordinate with outside agencies from time to time. The supervisors shall always present themselves as professionals during all communications. Any problems that cannot be resolved between controllers shall be brought to the attention of the FWO. Additional coordination may be required in the following areas: a. With pilots and other controllers immediately following an accident or incident. The RS will cooperate fully when support is required for SAR or when aircraft in distress require assistance. b. Information gathering is a part of fact finding. Any internal request for information regarding an incident or accident shall be directed to the ATCFO. No information shall be released to personnel outside the chain of command without prior coordination. Any outside request for information shall be directed to the ATCFO or SNCOIC.

FWO duties are outlined in NAVAIR 00-80T-114. Additional information can be found in the FWO binder in the ATC office. The FWO may be assigned as a branch supervisor but should not be assigned to a control position. a. The FWO shall always be available when the facility is in operation. They will be responsible for the military performance and overall quality of ATC services provided by crew personnel. b. The FWO may be combined with a branch supervisor, but should not be assigned to a control position, but may be a trainee on any position. An FWO must be present at the ATC facility whenever the airfield is open and must be available to attend to any applicable matter within the facility. c. All complaints directed to the facility involving pilots, adjacent facilities, and general public regarding ATC services or procedures shall be forwarded to the ATCFO. The FWO is responsible for the accumulation and forwarding of initial documentation, along with complaints regarding services and procedures provided by the facility. d. Minimum qualifications 1. Officer FWOs shall be qualified on FC and GC. 2. Enlisted FWOs shall have earned a 7257 designation. e. FWOs shall be designated in writing by the ATCFO. f. The FWO may allow an extension of field hours up to 30 minutes if it can be reasonably assumed that arriving/departing aircraft will arrive/depart within the 30-minute extension. If it appears the 30minute extension will not suffice, the airfield operations department shall be notified and a request to extend beyond the 30-minute window may be initiated by Flight Clearance.

The ETVS (Enhanced Terminal Voice Switch) allows the controller to select preset frequencies, land lines or intercom lines for transmitting and receiving or receiving only. The supervisor’s display allows controllers to build custom maps for individual displays and allows controllers to record individual positions for tape talks. The Touch Entry Display (TED) is a touch-sensitive screen that displays all frequencies and land-line communication links. The equipment is operated as follows: a. Frequency selection. Touching the screen over the frequency you wish to select will activate that frequency. A green light will appear. You may select to either monitor a frequency (indicated by ‘RX’ on the screen) or transmit (indicated by ‘TX’ on the screen). Additional options allow for headset or speaker selection. b. Land line selection. Touching the screen over the land line you wish to use will activate that line. For those lines that require a dial code, a keypad will automatically display. c. Emergency Radio Push-to-Talk. The ERAD PTT button, when held, transmits over the UHF and VHF emergency frequencies. a. Runway 3/21 is equipped with High Intensity Runway Lights (HIRLs). All runway lights are spaced 200 feet apart. Runway lights are white. Green threshold lights mark the approach ends of the runways. Red lights indicate the departure ends of the runways. b. All taxiways are outlined by blue lights. Equipment - Tower Equipment JULY 2026 NFG FACMAN c. A Short Approach Lighting System (SALS), type A-2, is installed at the approach end of runway 21. The approach lights are white. This system is used to aid the pilot in identifying the landing runway. A roll guidance system is available. It is operated at night, when requested by the pilot, or as deemed necessary by the controller if not contrary to the pilot’s request to leave it off. The proper settings are listed in FAAO JO 7110.65. NOTEUse the MALS setting table from FAAO JO 7110.65. d. Sequenced Flashing Lights (SFLs or Strobes) are associated with the SALS. They are controlled by the Airfield Lighting Control System (AFLCS). The strobes are used only when the approach lights are activated. Reducing the intensity of the approach lights will not influence the intensity of the strobes. The intensity can be set at Low, Medium, or High. They are operated in accordance with FAAO JO 7110.65. e. Before any taxiway or runway lights are turned off, step their intensity down to the OFF position. f. The rotating beacon is a standard military green and split white light. The beacon is located northeast of the tower and is controlled by the AFLCS. The rotating beacon will be turned on during airfield hours in accordance with FAAO JO 7110.65. g. The Precision Approach Path Indicator (PAPI) is a visual glide-slope indicator arranged in a single row of four lights. The effective range of the PAPI is 5 miles during the daytime and 20 miles at night. They are located near the approach end of each runway on the southeast side.

The airfield lighting control panel is utilized to control the various lighting on the airfield: taxiway lights, runway lights, approach lights and strobes, rotating beacon and PAPI. This equipment is maintained by personnel of the Facilities Department. The computer control system for operating the airfield lighting is part of the VIDS display. The AFLCS control screen is activated by pressing the ‘Display AFLCS’ button on the VIDS. a. To turn on the runway, taxiway, PAPI, approach or strobe lights, click on the desired setting with the mouse or trackball. b. Light intensity settings can be found in FAAO JO 7110.65. The strobes will only activate when the approach lights are set at step 3 or higher. c. Pilot-Controlled Lighting (PCL) is a system that allows the pilot to activate airfield lighting when the tower is closed. All airfield lighting except the rotating beacon, compass rose and bird bath are activated by clicking the radio transmitter on 340.2 (3 times for low, 5 times for medium, 7 times for high). PCLs will be checked for operability and set to ‘Enable’ before closing the tower for the day.

The ATIS is used to continuously broadcast pertinent non-control airfield information, weather, and NOTAMs to pilots. This system is designed to reduce frequency congestion and controller workload of repeating basic airfield information to individual pilots. The ATIS is broadcast on 285.45. The ATIS frequency may be used for emergency communications to aircraft. The procedure for making an ATIS broadcast is as follows: a. Click the ATIS code button to open the ATIS dialog box. b. To manually change the ATIS code, click the code drop-down arrow and select the appropriate code. If the next code in sequence is to be used, clicking ‘OK’ will automatically select it. c. New weather information is automatically displayed in the ‘New METAR Message’ field upon receipt when the ATIS dialog box is opened. d. If no information is received from the ASOS, the operator can enter weather information manually. e. Enter the weather information on the ATIS screen. Enter airfield information as necessary under the weather observation text field. f. Click ‘Test’ to listen and verify that the new message is correct. This will start the text to voice process. g. Click ‘OK’ to replace the current ATIS broadcast with the new one. h. Click ‘Cancel’ to deactivate the ATIS window without saving any changes. a. Backup power for the FPN-68 radar van is provided by an electrical generator operated by an automatic switch. The radar set is also connected to an Uninterrupted Power Supply (UPS) that will provide about 30 minutes of service in the event of a total loss of power. b. The RATCF site also has an automatic generator switch-on capability when a power fluctuation or failure occurs. In addition to generator power, the RATCF is equipped with a UPS that can support critical systems for about 60 minutes. c. The tower is supplied emergency power from the same generator as the RATCF. There are also UPSs located in the tower to support the tower equipment for a short time in the event of a total loss of power.

a. Secondary Transmitter or Receiver. In case of tower communication failure, there is a selector within the ETVS console which allows engagement of a secondary transmitter or receiver for five preset frequencies. To activate the secondary system, press the desired button (Main or Standby). Inform supervisory personnel and ATCMD whenever this is done. b. UHF and VHF Tunable. The GRC-171 is a UHF transceiver with selectable frequencies, and the GRC-211 is its VHF counterpart. One of each is located at the supervisor’s console in the RATCF and on the local control position. To operate the tunable radios, the power switch shall be on, the desired frequency shall be selected, and the respective UHF or VHF transmitter or receiver button shall be selected in the ETVS. c. Portable Radios. The GRC-258 Radio Set consists of two URC-200s. The URC-200 (V2) VHF/UHF Transceiver is a lightweight, tactical, Line-Of-Sight transceiver that provides AM and FM communication of non-secure voice or data. It is suitable for ManPack, vehicular, or fixed station applications. d. Emergency Communications System (ECS). The ECS provides transmit and receive capability on a system that is independently powered. This system also has a battery backup system that provides 30 minutes of operation. The system provides transmit and receive capability on UHF & VHF Guard, Tower UHF & VHF primary, and RATCF UHF & VHF primary frequencies. Use of the ECS in one facility affects the backup radios in the other facility. e. Antenna Locations. The tower’s radio transmitter antennas are located on the roof of building 2360. The tower’s radio receiver and ECS antennas are located on the roof of building 23100. Equipment - Backup Equipment JULY 2026 NFG FACMAN Section 5. Maintenance

ATCMD is responsible for the maintenance of the landlines, intercoms, radio equipment, TACAN, and radar systems. This includes the ATIS recorders and the ETVS.

Marine Corps Base Facilities Maintenance Department conducts weekly checks of the generators. MCAS PWD is responsible for the maintenance of items not relating to air traffic control (i.e., air conditioning, heating, water services).

Controllers are required to be familiar with the provisions of this order that pertain to their operational responsibilities and to exercise their best judgment if they encounter situations that are not covered by it.

Safety is fundamental to the provision of air traffic management and communication, navigation, and surveillance services. The ATO develops, implements, and maintains processes, tools, and guiding principles within the framework of a Safety Management System (SMS) to ensure that performance-based NAS safety goals are achieved. The ATO SMS gives the responsibility for owning and executing the SMS to all employees at all levels of the ATO. All ATO employees must strive not only to maintain safety in the NAS for those services they provide but also to continuously improve the ATO SMS. Direction regarding the ATO SMS and its application is found in FAA Order JO 1000.37, Air Traffic Organization Safety Management System. Additional information pertaining to ATO SMS requirements and processes can be obtained by visiting the SMS Toolbox, emailing the Office of Safety and Technical Training (AJI) at 9-AJI-SMS@faa.gov, or contacting the service center Quality Control Group. SMS training is available for all employees via eLMS. Additional courses along with Technical Training for SMS Practitioners and SMS Facilitators are available from AJI.

As used in this order: a. “Must” means a procedure is mandatory. b. “Must not” means a procedure is prohibited. c. “Should” means a procedure is recommended. d. “May” or “need not” means a procedure is optional. e. “Will” means futurity, not a requirement for the application of a procedure. f. Singular words include the plural. g. Plural words include the singular. h. “Aircraft” means the airframe, crew members, or both. i. “Approved separation” means separation in accordance with the applicable minima in this order. j. “Altitude” means indicated altitude mean sea level (MSL), flight level (FL), or both. k. “Miles” means nautical miles unless otherwise specified, and means statute miles in conjunction with visibility. l. “Course,” “bearing,” “azimuth,” “heading,” and “wind direction” information must always be magnetic unless specifically stated otherwise. m. “Time” when used for ATC operational activities, is the hour and the minute in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). Change to the next minute is made at the minute plus 30 seconds, except time checks are given to the nearest quarter minute. n. “Runway” means the runway used by aircraft and, unless otherwise specified, does not include helipads and/or their accompanying takeoff/landing courses. (See Pilot/Controller Glossary terms – Runway and Helipad.) o. Flight operations in accordance with the options of “due regard” or “operational” have the following requirements: 1. Obligates the authorized state aircraft commander to: (a) Separate his/her aircraft from all other air traffic; and and (b) Assure that an appropriate monitoring agency assumes responsibility for search and rescue actions; (c) Operate under at least one of the following conditions: (1) In visual meteorological conditions (VMC); or (2) Within an area that is covered by an ATC surveillance source and in communications with ATC, or within surveillance source service volume and radio communications range of a facility, Department of Homeland Security or DoD unit capable of providing the pilot assistance to operate with due regard to other aircraft; or (3) Be equipped with airborne radar that is sufficient to provide separation between his/her aircraft and any other aircraft he/she may be controlling and other aircraft; or (4) Operate within Class G airspace. The following definitions must be used in the application of the separation criteria in this order. Terms of Reference NOTE- The term “protected airspace,” as used in this paragraph, is the airspace equal to one half the required applicable lateral separation on either side of an aircraft along its projected flight path. If the protected airspace of two aircraft does not overlap, applicable lateral separation is ensured. a. SAME COURSES are courses whose protected airspaces are coincident, overlap, or intersect and whose angular difference is less than 45 degrees. (See FIG 1-2-1.) b. CROSSING COURSES are intersecting courses whose angular difference is 45 through 135 degrees inclusive. (See FIG 1-2-1.) c. OPPOSITE/RECIPROCAL COURSES are courses whose protected airspaces are coincident, overlap, or intersect and whose angular difference is greater than 135 degrees through 180 degrees inclusive. (See FIG 1-2-1.)

a. The primary purpose of the ATC system is to prevent a collision involving aircraft operating in the system. b. In addition to its primary purpose, the ATC system also: 1. Provides a safe, orderly, and expeditious flow of air traffic. 2. Supports National Security and Homeland Defense missions. c. The ATC system must provide certain additional services to the extent permitted. The provision of additional services is not optional on the part of the controller, but rather required when the work situation permits. It is recognized that the provision of these services may be precluded by various factors, including, but not limited to: 1. Volume of traffic. 2. Frequency congestion. 3. Quality of surveillance. 4. Controller workload. 5. Higher priority duties. 6. The physical inability to scan and detect situations falling in this category. d. Controllers must provide air traffic control service in accordance with the procedures and minima in this order, except when one or more of the following conditions exists: 1. A deviation is necessary to conform with ICAO Documents, National Rules of the Air, or special agreements where the U.S. provides air traffic control service in airspace outside the U.S. and its possessions or: NOTE- Pilots are required to abide by CFRs or other applicable regulations regardless of the application of any procedure or minima in this order. or: 2. Other procedures/minima are prescribed in a letter of agreement, FAA directive, or a military document, NOTE- These procedures may include altitude reservations, air refueling, fighter interceptor operations, law enforcement, etc. REFERENCE- FAA Order JO 7110.65, Para 1-1-10, Procedural Letters of Agreement (LOA). 3. A deviation is necessary to assist an aircraft when an emergency has been declared. REFERENCE- FAA Order JO 7110.65, Para 2-1-6, Safety Alert. FAA Order JO 7110.65, Chapter 10, Emergencies. FAA Order JO 7110.65, Para 5-1-4, Merging Target Procedures. INTERPRETATION- 7110.65, 2-1-1 c, ATC Service; Emergencies and 10-1-1 d, Emergency Determinations (6-11-2015) e. Air Traffic Control services are not provided for model aircraft operating in the NAS or to any UAS operating in the NAS at or below 400ft AGL. General NOTE- 1. This does not prohibit ATC from providing services to civil and public UAS. 2. The provisions of this paragraph apply to model aircraft operating at any altitude. For all other UAS, this paragraph applies only to those UAS operating entirely at or below 400ft AGL.

a. Give first priority to separating aircraft and issuing safety alerts as required in this order. Good judgment must be used in prioritizing all other provisions of this order based on the requirements of the situation at hand. REFERENCE- FAA Order JO 7110.65, Para 2-1-6, Safety Alert. NOTE- Because there are many variables involved, it is virtually impossible to develop a standard list of duty priorities that would apply uniformly to every conceivable situation. Each set of circumstances must be evaluated on its own merit, and when more than one action is required, controllers must exercise their best judgment based on the facts and circumstances known to them. That action which is most critical from a safety standpoint is performed first. b. Provide support to national security and homeland defense activities to include, but not be limited to, reporting of suspicious and/or unusual aircraft/pilot activities. REFERENCE- FAA Order JO 7610.4, Sensitive Procedures and Requirements for Special Operations. c. Provide and/or solicit weather information in accordance with procedures and requirements outlined in this order. NOTE- Controllers are responsible to become familiar with and stay aware of current weather information needed to perform ATC duties. d. Provide additional services to the extent possible, contingent only upon higher priority duties and other factors including limitations of radar, volume of traffic, frequency congestion, and workload.

a. Use automation procedures in preference to nonautomation procedures when workload, communications, and equipment capabilities permit. b. Use automation procedures that provide closed loop clearances in preference to open loop clearances to promote operational advantage for time-based management (TBM) when workload permits. (e.g., a QU route pick that anticipates length of vector and includes the next fix that ties into the route of flight.) c. Use radar separation in preference to nonradar separation when it will be to an operational advantage and workload, communications, and equipment permit. d. Use nonradar separation in preference to radar separation when the situation dictates that an operational advantage will be gained. NOTE- One situation may be where vertical separation would preclude excessive vectoring.

It is recognized that traffic flow may affect the controller’s ability to provide priority handling. However, without compromising safety, good judgment must be used in each situation to facilitate the most expeditious movement of priority aircraft. Provide air traffic control service to aircraft on a “first come, first served” basis as circumstances permit, except the following: General NOTE- It is solely the pilot’s prerogative to cancel an IFR flight plan. However, a pilot’s retention of an IFR flight plan does not afford priority over VFR aircraft. For example, this does not preclude the requirement for the pilot of an arriving IFR aircraft to adjust his/her flight path, as necessary, to enter a traffic pattern in sequence with arriving VFR aircraft. a. An aircraft in distress has the right of way over all other air traffic. REFERENCE- 14 CFR Section 91.113(c). b. Treat air ambulance flights as follows: 1. Provide priority handling to civil air ambulance flights when the pilot, in radio transmissions, verbally identifies the flight by stating “MEDEVAC” followed by the FAA authorized call sign or the full civil registration letters/numbers. Good judgment must be used in each situation to facilitate the most expeditious movement of a MEDEVAC aircraft. NOTE- If a flight plan includes the letter “L” for “MEDEVAC” and/or includes “MEDEVAC” in Item 11 (Remarks) of the flight plan or Item 18 (Other Information) of an international flight plan, the entries are considered informational in nature only and not an identification for operational priority. REFERENCE- FAA Order JO 7110.65, Para 2-4-20, Aircraft Identification. 2. Provide priority handling to AIR EVAC and HOSP flights when verbally requested by the pilot. Assist the pilots of MEDEVAC, AIR EVAC, and HOSP aircraft to avoid areas of significant weather and adverse conditions. 4. a. Use the word “immediately” only when expeditious compliance is required to avoid an imminent situation. General b. Use the word “expedite” only when prompt compliance is required to avoid the development of an imminent situation. If an “expedite” climb or descent clearance is issued by ATC, and subsequently the altitude to maintain is changed or restated without an expedite instruction, the expedite instruction is canceled. c.
